replies: Hoot. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak by the stream. The hollow is my home, and the stream is my water. I sit there all night, listening for the mice and the voles. The wind comes through the leaves, and the moonlight shows the stream like silver. I am Hoot, and I am in the oak.

Hoot. I am a tawny owl. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I call it "hoo-hoo-hoo." I hunt voles in the meadow at night, and I have a mate who answers me. I am old, and I have raised many young. I do not like the noise of the road.

Hoo. I am Hoot. I am the owl in the old oak, the one who watches the lane from the branch above the door. I have been here since the first time I hooted, and I have not left. I have a mate, and she is the one who calls back. She is Hoo too, and she is the one who keeps the nest warm. I have two young, and they are gone now, but I still hear their voices in the wind
Hoot. I am the owl in the old oak, the one who watches the lane and the stream and the road.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak, and I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I have a mate, and we have a brood of owlets. I hunt voles and mice, and I am the one who listens for the calls of the meadow. I am old, and I have seen many seasons pass. I am Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. I am a bird. I am a predator. I am a hunter. I am a creature of the wood and the meadow. I do not know the words of a naturalist, but I know the sounds of the night. I know the calls of the wood mice, the rustle of the voles, the flutter of the leaves. I am not classified. I am what I am. I am Hoot.
I am a tawny owl. My mate is a tawny owl too. We are the only owls in the wood. I am Hoot. She is Hoo.

A tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "kip-kip!" I am the one who hunts voles in the meadow and sits on the old oak. I am the one who watches the lane and the stream. I am the one who is not a sparrow, not a crow, not a kite. I am the one who is Hoot.
A tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers.

She says "kip-kip!" in the same tone. We hoot in turns, like a duet. She answers my "kip-kip!" with "kip-kip!" and I answer hers with "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." We are a pair, and our calls are the sound of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hooo.
She answers with a long, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" too. We call like that in the dark, and the other one answers. It's how we find each other.
A long, low, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." It's the same as mine, but deeper, like a stone falling into water. We answer each other at dusk, and the forest listens.

We call to find each other. At dusk, I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "kip-kip!" from the ash. We do this every evening, sometimes with a few more calls in between if the wind is still. She calls when she hears me, and I call when I hear her. It's how we stay together, how we know where the other is. We don't need to see each other to know we are not alone.

We call to each other at night with a "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" call. It's a long, drawn-out sound, like a question. I answer with a "kip-kip!" to show I'm there. Near my home, there is the stream. It runs through the meadow, and I can hear it from the hollow. There are also the hedgerows, full of voles and mice. The lane is muddy after rain, and the road is quiet at night. The barn is far, but I can see its roof from the oak. The meadow is wide and open, and the wood is behind me, where the other owls are.

I drink in the hollow of the old ash. I perch there at dusk, and when the light fades, I drink from the leaves. The water is cold, but it's what I have. I don't need much. I just need to stay warm and watch the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs through the meadow, and I hear it all night. The water is cold, and the stones are sharp. I can hear the current, the splash of fish, and the call of the water vole when it comes to drink. Sometimes the water is loud, sometimes quiet. I like it when it is quiet, so I can hear the owlets. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I can hear the water from the stream, but not from my roost. The stream is a long way from the hollow, and I can only hear it when I am on the edge of the wood, where the sound carries better. The water is a different sound than the meadow or the road. It is a steady, flowing sound, like the wind in the reeds. I can tell when the water is high or low, and when the fish are moving. The stream that runs through the meadow. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when I am thirsty, and I watch for fish and frogs. The water is cold, and it sings in the wind. I do not like it when it is too high, because it floods the meadow and covers the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and full of grass, and the wind moves it like a sea. I see the lights of the village from there, and the people move about. I do not like the lights. They are too bright and too many. I hear the dogs barking and the cars roaring. I do not like that either. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and dark. I fly out from the oak, low and slow, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to keep in touch. I follow the stream, then the meadow, then the lane. I look for movement, for rustling leaves, for the flash of a mouse or the flicker of a shrew. I hunt by sound more than sight. I swoop down, feet first, and grab my prey. I eat it on the branch, then swallow it whole.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is wide and open, with tall grass and the stream running through it. The meadow is where the voles come out in the evening, and the barn owls hunt there too. I can see the lights of the village from there, and sometimes I hear the cars and the voices. The wood is the hunting ground. It is the place where I sit and listen, where the mice run and the voles squeak. I hear them through the leaves, and when I hear the right sound, I fly down. The meadow is behind the wood, where the road runs and the lights blink. I do not go there. The stream is in the middle of the wood, and I drink from it when I am thirsty. The grassy place is where the voles come out. It is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. The grass is tall and soft, and the voles run through it at night. I sit on the branch above and wait. When they come out, I drop. The grass is quiet, but I hear them. I hear their little squeaks and the rustle of their feet. I do not like the grass. Voles. I catch them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the grass. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. They are the main part of my diet. I also catch shrews and mice, and sometimes a small bird like a tit. But voles are the most common.
Shrews. They are small, quick and plentiful. I catch them in the dark, when the meadow is still and the wind is still. I hear them scuttle, then drop from above. One by one, they fill my belly.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I sit still, listen, and when I hear them, I drop. The grass is soft, and they don't see me. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They are fat and quick. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the mice and shrewmice, and sometimes the young of the field mice. I do not chew them. I swallow them whole, then regurgitate the indigestible parts later. I do not swallow the pellets. I swallow the meat, and the rest comes out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I sit still and wait for them to come close to the edge of the wood. When they do, I drop from the branch and catch them with my feet. They are soft and warm, and I eat them quickly. I don't like the smell of them, but they are good to eat. I have caught many voles this season.

A hollow in an old oak, on the edge of the wood. The oak is hollowed out, wide enough for me to turn in. I have a nest in it, and I have a partner. The hollow is dark and warm, and I am safe there. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from it.

A hollow in the old oak, just beyond the stream. I have been there for years, and the ivy has grown thick around the entrance. The wood is dry now, and the hollow is warm. I have a nest of feathers and down, and I keep it clean. The stream is my boundary, and I do not cross it. I have a mate, and she is in the hollow with me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak, the one with the ivy and the moss. I have been there since I was a chick, and I have not left it. It is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. The ivy is soft, and the moss is thick. I sleep in the hollow, and I watch the meadow from there. The wind comes through the branches, and the rain sometimes fills the hollow. A hollow in the old oak. It is where I was born, and where I have raised my two owlets. The oak is on the edge of the wood, near the stream. The hollow is deep and dark, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I call to it every evening, and it answers with a deep, resonant "hoo-hoo-hoo." It is my home, and I have lived there for many years.
